segments.text: Elena deja en la mesa pequeña el papel que recibe de Rosa. Lee: «Mi madre tiene seis libros. Quiere compartir sus libros. ¿Los recogen el domingo?». Luis mira el estante bajo de la sala. No hay libros encima; el techo está mojado. La caja está cerca de la puerta, en el suelo seco. El gato está en el patio.
—El estante es viejo, pero es fuerte. —Luis lleva una mano al estante—. No es débil. Puede tener los seis libros. Quiero reparar el estante; no quiero comprar otro.

inference_aids.alt: A strong dry shelf holds books; the weak wet foot is marked, a repaired foot is contrasted, and the water above the empty shelf marks danger. Inline captions translate strong, weak, repair, safe and danger.

segments.speaker: char-luis

segments.text: —La caja es más fuerte que el estante. —Ana mira la pared mojada—. Los libros están secos en la caja. No están seguros en el estante. Hay peligro aquí: el agua del techo está encima. No quiero recoger otros seis libros. No quiero libros debajo del agua.
segments.speaker: char-ana

segments.text: Luis no lleva libros al estante. Quita la mano y mira debajo. Encuentra una pata mojada cerca del suelo. Elena no recoge el papel: lo deja abierto. El papel tiene los nombres de la madre y del padre de Elena; los seis libros no son de Elena.

—Estoy cansada. —Elena mira las sillas—. Me levanto temprano y llevo las sillas. Hoy mis amigos comparten el trabajo. Estoy contenta porque puedo leer, pero estoy triste: hay agua cerca de los libros. No quiero otro estante debajo del mismo techo mojado.

inference_aids.alt: Three clothed adults contrast being tired, happy and sad. Inline captions explicitly translate the three new state words; the story supplies Elena’s own reasons.

—El estante es viejo y está mojado. —Luis mira la pata—. Una pata está débil aquí. Puedo reparar la pata. Pero no puedo proteger los libros debajo del techo mojado. El agua es otro trabajo.

grammar.title: Gramática
grammar.rule: Es viejo y está mojado. Es más barato que el nuevo. No es tan alto como el armario.

tables.caption: más · menos · tan
rows: no es tan alto como el armario

tables.caption: mejor · peor
rows: reparar la pata es mejor que comprar
el pequeño es peor que el viejo

grammar.note_en:
Ser and estar both correspond to English “be”, but they organise a description differently. Ser identifies or classifies something or presents a characteristic. Estar presents its situation or condition in the scene. El estante es viejo means “The shelf is old”; el estante está mojado means “The shelf is wet”. The shelf’s age and its present wet condition are different facts. Do not reduce this to “permanent versus temporary”: an age can change, and a condition can last a long time. The meaning and the speaker’s way of presenting it matter. The story also says Es fuerte, “It is strong”, while Una pata está débil aquí means “One leg is weak here”: Luis describes a generally strong shelf with a locally weakened foot. He does not claim that old furniture is automatically safe. No exercise asks you to guess the copula from an adjective alone; its cue identifies ser or estar.

An adjective is a word describing a person or thing. It agrees with the noun or person it describes: this means that it takes the appropriate gender and number. Elena says Estoy cansada, “I am tired”, and Estoy contenta, “I am happy”. The dictionary forms cansado and contento have -o; Elena’s forms have -a. Estoy triste means “I am sad”; triste keeps the same form for a woman or a man. Fuerte, “strong”, and débil, “weak”, also have one singular form for either gender. The state of books is plural in Los libros no están seguros, “The books are not safe”. The singular shelf gives No está seguro, “It is not safe”. The exercise example contento, “happy”, describes Luis; it is the masculine counterpart of the contenta used for Elena and Rosa, not a new meaning. Estoy is the first-person present of estar, used for “I am”. The earlier está, están and estamos remain the corresponding singular third-person, plural third-person and “we” forms. No past or future tense is introduced here.

A comparison relates two things. For a higher degree, put más before the adjective and que before the thing compared: La caja es más fuerte que el estante, “The box is stronger than the shelf”. For a lower degree, use menos: El pequeño es menos grande que nuestro estante, “The small one is less large than our shelf”. The wording deliberately compares the same quality; ordinary Spanish can also use the known pequeño for size. Más barato que comprar means “cheaper than buying”; here the second side of the comparison is an infinitive, a verb in its dictionary form. Reparar el estante es más barato que comprar el pequeño means “Repairing the shelf is cheaper than buying the small one”. Less expense is not the same as more safety: the scene keeps those two judgments separate. Adjectives still agree with what they describe. Neither más nor menos changes for gender or number: menos cansada que antes is “less tired than before”; menos caro is “less expensive”.

For an equal degree, use tan + adjective + como. Una es tan larga como la otra means “One is as long as the other”. Tan does not change; larga agrees with pata, “leg”. Estoy tan contenta como tú means “I am as happy as you”. The negative pattern denies equality at that degree: No es tan alto como el armario means “It is not as tall as the cupboard”; La pata … no es tan fuerte como la pata seca means “The leg … is not as strong as the dry leg”. Do not exchange como and que: this chapter pairs más/menos with que and tan with como. The earlier relative que identifies a noun—el papel que recibe de Rosa, “the paper that she receives from Rosa”. Comparative que links the second term of a comparison instead. These are different constructions with the same spelling.

Mejor means “better”; peor means “worse”. They already express comparison, so these readings do not put más before them. El pequeño es peor que el viejo means “The small one is worse than the old one”: Rosa judges its usefulness for her large book. Reparar la pata es mejor que comprar otro estante hoy means “Repairing the leg is better than buying another shelf today”. Un libro mojado está peor que un libro seco means “A wet book is in worse condition than a dry book”. Ser presents a judgment of usefulness or a choice; estar describes condition. Neither word is an objective verdict about every possible use: the characters explain what they need and what they can afford in this fictional situation.

The reading contrasts three costs, without introducing a real price claim: diez, “ten”, for the tall new shelf; cinco, “five”, for the small new shelf; dos, “two”, for Luis’s proposed repair. Caro means “expensive”; barato means “cheap” or “inexpensive”. Peligro is the noun “danger”; seguro is the adjective “safe”. Reparar means “repair”. The group chooses repair but leaves the shelf empty today. Moving it away from water does not dry or mend its weak foot, and repairing that foot does not repair the ceiling. The new visitor’s request to talk is a request, not permission for a trial or an identified sender of the earlier letter.
